title: A grand strategy game on a 163K-tile planet, written solo in native C++ and Vulkan with Claude Code
author: Magistairs
selftext:
I've spent the last several months building Orbis, a grand strategy game that plays out a whole civilization's history on a procedurally generated planet of 163,000 tiles, all native C++ with a hand-written Vulkan renderer and no engine under it, made solo with Claude Code on the code while I drive the design, and it runs on both Windows and Linux.

163K tiles is a lot, and the reason it holds up is that the simulation runs on its own thread fully decoupled from rendering, so the planet can be churning through trade and wars and migrations across every tile while the framerate doesn't care how much is happening, and getting that lock-free threading right in raw C++ is the kind of thing that would normally eat a solo dev alive but gets a lot more doable with an AI that actually understands memory ordering next to you.

What keeps it from turning into mush is that nearly every system started as a failing integration test before any code existed, so trade, diplomacy, war, worker allocation all have a guard behind them, and when an agent quietly breaks something three files away a test goes red the same minute instead of a month later. Most days I'm running four agents at once across four git worktrees so they never step on each other, each on a single system on its own branch, all reviewed and tested before they merge rather than going wide and refactoring half the codebase.

The game itself: population is your only currency, no gold and no tech tree, so cities grow out of actual people and end up fighting over land because more farmland means less housing and you can't just sprawl forever, while the AI states run on behavior trees for their own war and diplomacy and production, and your job is to influence rather than command and watch a few thousand years play out.

It's free, a 3.7 MB download with no installer, Windows and Linux, very much an alpha and more sandbox than finished game right now, and I'd genuinely love to hear what felt interesting or made no sense: [https://magistairs.itch.io/orbis](https://magistairs.itch.io/orbis)

comments.author: Aromatic-Low-4578
comments.body:
This is very cool but I wouldn't call it 'hand-written' when claude wrote it. 

Still, one of the more interesting projects I've seen here. Will be excited to follow its development.

replies.author: Magistairs
replies.body:
True, it was to oppose to "bundled", I changed to "custom" ;)

Thanks for the comments!

BTW as you can see from the screenshots, UI and rendering are clearly the most difficult parts for Claude!

comments.author: SquirrelTomahawk
comments.body: Hey brother could i message u for assistance? Im also trying to build a map strategy game but struggling a bit

replies.author: Magistairs
replies.body:
Of course! 

One thing I learned though: strategy games are not for solo devs, even with Claude, they just have too many systems and dependencies and any balance issue can break the whole game.

It has to be simple like a 4x with only a few selected core features

comments.author: PictureOld8923
comments.body:
Great concept but too text heavy imho

Even if the gameplay is great you don't need triple a visuals but some smart balance is still expected unless you're going for a very narrow niche

replies.author: Magistairs
replies.body:
Do you mean the UI? Yes one of my main problem is imGui, Claude is not good with it while it can generate nice icons and effects in HTML/CSS

About the game itself, it's heavily inspired by Paradox Interactive games, they are niche indeed and text heavy as well, I'm using some of their common QoL features like macro builder, nested tooltips and heatmaps overlays

comments.author: Former-Objective-272
comments.body: Also using Claude Code but with Rust/Bevy instead of C++. The compiler catching AI generated nonsense before runtime has been the biggest win. Have you run into issues with Claude generating plausible looking C++ that compiles but has subtle logic bugs?

replies.author: Magistairs
replies.body: I don't think I've seen C++ mistakes, the game is full of bugs of course but it's usually either Claude missing context (one variable changed on one side, it doesn't know what is done on another side and is too lazy to check) or adding subfeatures I didn't ask for when I discussed a design
